paper.title: Correcting Guided Diffusion Trajectories with Spectral Alignment
paper.abstract: Abstract The practical success of conditional image generation hinges on fine-grained differences in condition alignment and visual fidelity. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is central to this success, but its lack of an explicit criterion makes it difficult to assess whether the guided trajectory is progressing as intended. To address this gap, we show that spectral alignment provides a principled criterion for understanding guidance behavior and improving guided diffusion sampling through adaptive correction. Our analysis identifies the spectra of intermediate states as an indicator of consistency with the expected spectral evolution of the forward process. Based on this observation, we introduce Spectral Correction Guidance , a method that corrects deviations from an analytic reference spectrum during sampling. The proposed method is training-free and applicable across diffusion backbones and conditional generation tasks without modifying the underlying model. Experiments demonstrate consistent gains in preference-based metrics over baseline guidance methods in text-to-image generation and improved generation quality over CFG on ImageNet. These improvements persist across a range of guidance scales and with fewer denoising steps. Our analyses and ablations provide insight into guidance behavior and how the proposed method affects generation quality.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Denoising diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) have shown strong generative capabilities across diverse domains ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) , including image synthesis ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ; Karras et al., 2022 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) . They exhibit stable convergence during training while modeling the reverse of a forward noising process that perturbs clean data toward a noise distribution. The learned reverse process captures rich data distributions, enabling sample generation through denoising from high to low noise levels. Building on this capability, diffusion models support open-ended conditional generation tasks such as text-to-image synthesis ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . Classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) has become a standard technique for steering sampling toward the target condition in diffusion models. As illustrated in Figures 1(a) and 1(b) , conditional sampling without guidance often fails to capture the target condition, whereas CFG improves both condition alignment and perceptual quality. These benefits depend on how guidance is applied along the denoising trajectory ( Hong et al., 2023 ; Karras et al., 2024 ; Sadat et al., 2024 ) . However, standard CFG uses a fixed guidance scale, limiting its ability to provide appropriate guidance at each denoising step ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) . Recent guidance methods aim to enhance the benefits of CFG while mitigating its adverse effects. They adjust the guidance strength across timesteps ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Malarz et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2025a ) , modify the direction of guidance with geometric constraints ( Sadat et al., 2025a ; Chung et al., 2024 ; Kwon et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2025b ) , or modulate guidance within predefined frequency bands ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Sadat et al., 2025b ; Song et al., 2026 ) . However, these benefits may not extend beyond the settings these methods are designed to address, such as high-guidance regimes. In Section 6.1 , experimental results show that these methods yield limited gains across a range of generation settings, where vanilla CFG remains a strong baseline. In this paper, we argue that these limitations arise from reliance on constraints or suppression rules without a criterion to guide correction along the denoising trajectory. However, defining such a criterion is challenging in the conventional spatial domain, since coordinate-based representations encode local structures and reflect sample-specific characteristics. To address this difficulty, we identify alignment between the power spectra of guided intermediate states and the expected spectra under the forward process as a key indicator of effective guidance. This provides a complementary perspective, capturing global patterns of diffusion dynamics along the denoising trajectory. Building on this observation, we propose Spectral Correction Guidance , a training-free method for correcting guided denoising trajectories according to the spectral dynamics of the diffusion process. We derive a criterion from the power-law spectral statistics of natural images ( Ruderman, 1997 ) , yielding a distributional reference that is not tied to individual samples or specific failure patterns. Based on this criterion, our method corrects deviations from the expected spectral behavior in intermediate states. The proposed correction enables adaptive adjustments across frequencies and timesteps without relying on a prescribed correction pattern. We further validate our method through extensive experiments on diverse conditional image generation tasks. In text-to-image generation, the proposed correction improves preference-based metrics across multiple backbones and guidance settings, indicating better text alignment and visual quality. In class-conditional generation, our method achieves lower FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and higher Inception Score ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) than CFG, even with fewer sampling steps. These results demonstrate that correcting spectral deviations during sampling can improve generation quality without additional training. Ablation studies examine how correction strength and the timestep range over which correction is applied affect generation outputs. We also discuss how the proposed method relates to existing guidance approaches from a spectral perspective. sections.heading: 3 Spectral Dynamics in the Diffusion Process

sections.heading: 5 A Spectral View of Existing Guidance Methods
sections.text: In this section, we discuss related guidance strategies. From a spectral perspective, we also examine how these strategies control distinct aspects of the guidance signal during denoising.

sections.heading: Scheduled guidance scaling.
sections.text: Scheduled guidance scaling replaces the constant guidance scale w w with a predefined timestep-dependent schedule. Kynkäänniemi et al. (2024) restrict guidance to selected denoising intervals, while Malarz et al. (2025) and Jin et al. (2025a) adjust the guidance strength according to predefined functional forms. By Parseval’s theorem, adjusting the guidance scale at each timestep also modulates the Fourier-domain energy of the guidance term. In this sense, our method provides fine-grained scaling through spectral correction at each timestep and frequency.

sections.heading: Geometry-aware guidance.
sections.text: Geometry-aware guidance methods constrain the magnitude ( Jin et al., 2025b ) or direction ( Sadat et al., 2025a ) of guided updates, or adjust sampling to reduce deviations from the data manifold ( Chung et al., 2024 ; Kwon et al., 2025 ) . Our method shares the goal of keeping guided trajectories consistent with the data distribution, but approaches it through spectral alignment with the forward marginals encountered during training.

sections.heading: Frequency-based guidance.
sections.text: Frequency-based methods modulate guidance using predefined frequency partitions ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , applying different guidance strengths to separate bands ( Sadat et al., 2025b ) or suppressing selected frequencies ( Song et al., 2026 ) . Although these methods also consider spectral information, their adjustments follow band-specific rules. In contrast, our method adapts the correction at each frequency based on spectral deviations from an analytic reference. sections.heading: Experimental setup.
sections.text: We evaluate our method on text-to-image and class-conditional image generation. For text-to-image generation, we compare against standard CFG ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) and representative methods from Section 5 : TV-CFG ( Jin et al., 2025a ) , CFG++ ( Chung et al., 2024 ) , and LF-CFG ( Song et al., 2026 ) . We use 10K prompts sampled from the COCO validation set ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . To assess generality across backbones, we conduct experiments with SDXL ( Podell et al., 2023 ) , PixArt- α \alpha ( Chen et al., 2023 ) , and SD3.5 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) . We evaluate each model at its default guidance scale and at a higher guidance scale. For class-conditional generation, we use DiT-XL/2 ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) and evaluate robustness across different numbers of sampling steps. We generate 50 samples per ImageNet class, resulting in 50K samples in total. Unless otherwise specified, all methods use the same prompts, labels, sampling budget, and guidance scales, and follow the recommended settings for each method.

sections.heading: Evaluation metrics.
sections.text: For text-to-image generation, we assess human preference using HPSv3 ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) , and HPSv2 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , text-image alignment using CLIP-T ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , and distributional matching using FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and sFID ( Nash et al., 2021 ) . We complement these metrics with a human preference study. For class-conditional generation, we follow the ADM evaluation protocol ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) and report FID, sFID, Inception Score (IS) ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) , Precision, and Recall to evaluate generation quality and distributional coverage across sampling budgets measured by the number of function evaluations (NFEs). sections.heading: Text-to-image generation.
sections.text: Table 1 presents quantitative results comparing our method with guidance baselines under their standard guidance settings. Standard CFG outperforms the other baseline methods on most preference-based metrics across the three backbones, indicating limited gains from existing guidance strategies at standard guidance scales. Our method improves on this strong baseline, achieving the highest HPSv3, ImageReward, and PickScore across all three models, along with the best or joint-best HPSv2 scores. Even on SD3.5, where standard CFG already achieves strong preference scores, our method yields additional gains. For distributional metrics, our method achieves the lowest FID and sFID on SDXL and the lowest FID on PixArt- α \alpha . Although TV-CFG and LF-CFG achieve lower FID and sFID on SD3.5, this comes with lower preference scores. Figure 5 provides qualitative support for the trends in Table 1 . In the SDXL examples, most methods produce plausible images, although LF-CFG shows weaker prompt alignment. CFG introduces a visible artifact around the front part of the airplane, which is alleviated by our method and CFG++. For PixArt- α \alpha , although other guidance variants provide some improvements, our method shows clearer gains in overall appearance and brightness balance. In the SD3.5 examples, CFG++ produces over-smoothed images, consistent with its lower quantitative scores. The remaining methods achieve similar overall quality, but our method produces more distinct fine-grained details. Furthermore, we evaluate our method under different guidance regimes. Table 2 demonstrates that our method improves over CFG at higher guidance scales. The improvement is clear for SD3.5, where our method maintains strong image quality and alignment while CFG becomes more sensitive to the increased guidance scale. As shown in Figure 6 , the larger guidance scale can lead to over-saturated images or weaker prompt following, whereas our method mitigates these effects and recovers more faithful compositions. Table 9 also shows that our method improves under lower guidance, while existing guidance methods show limited gains. These results indicate that the proposed correction provides stable guidance control across models and guidance scales. We provide a human preference study, multi-seed experiments and runtime measurements in the appendix. sections.heading: Class-conditional image generation.
sections.text: To evaluate our method across conditional generation tasks, we apply the proposed correction to class-conditional generation with DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet. As shown in Table 3 , our method achieves strong performance with the default 250 denoising steps. In particular, it reduces sFID from 7.42 to 4.92 and improves FID, Precision, and IS. Figure 7 shows that these quantitative gains are reflected in image quality. In the chameleon example, the proposed correction leads to a clearer depiction of the target class. The improvement is also visible in the jellyfish and space shuttle examples, where our method produces brighter and sharper images than the blurrier or darker CFG samples. The proposed method maintains strong performance across sampling budgets, with NFEs ranging from 250 to 25. Even with 50 NFEs, our method achieves an FID of 2.88 and an sFID of 6.29, matching the FID and improving upon the sFID of CFG with 250 NFEs. At 25 NFEs, our method remains competitive with CFG using 100 NFEs. Recall is slightly lower than CFG across budgets, indicating a trade-off between coverage and the observed gains in precision and fidelity. These results demonstrate that the proposed correction improves generation quality across sampling budgets and extends to conditional generation tasks beyond text-to-image synthesis.

sections.heading: Correction relaxation.
sections.text: The previous ablation shows that increasing correction strength improves fidelity and prompt alignment but can introduce artifacts. We thus study how to relax the correction across the denoising process to retain its benefits while reducing artifacts. Motivated by the role of late denoising steps in fine-grained detail formation ( Karras et al., 2021 ) , we vary the relaxation parameter ρ \rho , which controls when the frequency-domain constraint is relaxed during denoising. Figure 9 shows that applying correction until the end can retain artifacts, whereas applying it only in the early stage weakens its effect. An intermediate relaxation point provides the best balance between spectral correction and natural detail formation. We therefore adopt this setting in our final method. The relaxation analysis clarifies where spectral correction improves generation quality and where its continued application can degrade quality ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2025a ) .

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we demonstrated that spectral alignment can serve as a practical criterion for understanding guidance behavior and improving guided diffusion sampling through principled correction. This perspective provides a basis for assessing whether guided trajectories remain consistent with the spectral dynamics induced by the forward process. We derived an analytic reference from natural image statistics and used it to correct spectral deviations along guided denoising trajectories. Building on this criterion, Spectral Correction Guidance is a training-free method applicable to diverse diffusion backbones and conditional generation tasks without modifying the underlying model. Experiments show that the proposed method improves generation quality across model architectures, guidance strengths, and reduced sampling budgets, while prior guidance strategies provide limited gains in common guidance settings. This work highlights how diffusion dynamics and domain-specific statistics can be combined to establish a principled criterion for trajectory correction.

sections.heading: Appendix C Ethics Statement
sections.text: Generative modeling can support creative and practical applications, including image editing, design, and content creation. At the same time, improvements in generation quality can increase the risk of misuse, including harmful synthetic content. We therefore emphasize the need for responsible deployment policies.

sections.heading: Appendix D Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: The proposed method demonstrates that spectral alignment based on power spectra can provide a useful criterion for guiding diffusion trajectories and improving generation quality. However, this criterion only captures marginal frequency-domain statistics and does not fully characterize the generated distribution. Matching power spectra can align the overall spectral energy across frequencies, but it does not account for phase information or spatial structure. Future work could extend spectral correction beyond power spectra by using wavelet representations ( Mallat, 1989 ) to capture localized frequency structure and by incorporating constraints that account for phase and individual sample structure. Another limitation is that our correction is applied with a shared rule across samples and conditions. In practice, the amount and type of guidance needed may depend on the input condition, prompt, or class. Guidance strategies that adapt to the input condition ( Galashov et al., 2026 ; Papalampidi et al., 2026 ) suggest a promising direction for extending spectral correction to account for differences across samples and conditions. Combining spectral alignment with condition-aware guidance control could enable more flexible adjustment of the denoising trajectory.

sections.heading: Implementation details of our method.
sections.text: We apply the proposed correction at every denoising step, as described in Algorithm 1 . For text-to-image generation, we use 64 radial bins. The correction strength is set to λ = 0.05 \lambda=0.05 for SDXL and PixArt- α \alpha , and λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 for SD3.5. The relaxation factor is set to ρ = 0.5 \rho=0.5 for SDXL and SD3.5. For PixArt- α \alpha at the higher guidance scale, we use λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 and ρ = 0.5 \rho=0.5 , reflecting the need for stronger correction under stronger guidance. We estimate the target spectrum using the same inference-time sampling schedule as the one used for generation. For the DiT-XL/2 class-conditional experiments, we use 32 radial bins and set λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 across all sampling budgets. We add a small constant ε \varepsilon to the numerator and denominator of the spectrum ratio for numerical stability. To model the z 0 z_{0} space of each model, we encode COCO val 50K images ( Lin et al., 2014 ) into the corresponding latent space and fit the power-law curve based on Eq. 7 . We note that this fitting step is not essential to the method. It is a practical choice for setting the reference spectrum in our experiments. Since the reference spectrum is parameterized by only three scalar values, the corresponding power-law parameters can also be tuned without using external data. For the conceptual validation in Section 3 , we use 1,000 image–caption pairs from COCO val 50K. We use SDXL with 50 denoising steps, resolution 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 , and fp16 inference. For each sample, we encode the real image into the SDXL VAE latent space and measure the spectrum along the forward noising trajectory. We then run reverse denoising from random Gaussian noise using the corresponding caption as the prompt, and measure the spectrum of the generated trajectory. We evaluate CFG scales { 2.5 , 5.0 , 7.5 , 15.0 } \{2.5,5.0,7.5,15.0\} , together with unconditional and conditional baselines. To obtain the reported curve, we first average the spectra over the 1,000 samples for each trajectory type, and then compute the mean squared error between the log-power spectra. Thus, the comparison is performed between aggregate spectra rather than as a pairwise per-sample distance. Our method is training-free and does not require additional model training. All reported experiments were conducted on NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs. For class-conditional ImageNet experiments, generating 50K samples was parallelized over 15 GPUs and took approximately 8 hours. For text-to-image experiments, generating 10K samples was parallelized over 5 GPUs and took approximately 12 hours. sections.text: We first evaluate our method on SiT-XL/2 ( Ma et al., 2024 ) . We use 32 radial bins for power spectrum estimation, with λ = 0.005 \lambda=0.005 and ρ = 0.5 \rho=0.5 . sections.text: We also evaluate our method on JiT-L/16 ( Li and He, 2025 ) . We use 128 radial bins for power spectrum estimation, with λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 and ρ = 0.5 \rho=0.5 . The observation suggests that, although our method is motivated by spectral assumptions in pixel space, compressed latent spaces may provide a more stable domain for applying the correction by reducing sample-level spectral variability. sections.heading: Appendix N Additional Analysis of Power Spectrum Modeling
sections.text: Our method extends a spectral principle from pixel space to latent space. To empirically validate this assumption, we examine whether the power-law behavior of natural image spectra is preserved after encoding images into the latent spaces of the models used in our experiments. Figure 13 shows the mean power spectrum of encoded COCO val 50K images ( Lin et al., 2014 ) in the latent space of each model, along with the fitted curve based on Eq. 7 . The fitted curves achieve R 2 > 0.99 R^{2}>0.99 across models, indicating that the z 0 z_{0} spaces of the image generation models considered in our experiments can be well characterized by this power-law structure. This result provides empirical justification for applying the proposed spectral correction in these spaces. We also analyze the effect of binning resolution when estimating the power spectrum for the proposed correction. The binning resolution determines how many frequency components are grouped into each radial bin. To make the effect of this design choice more visible, we vary the number of radial bins under a relatively strong correction strength of λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 . Figure 14 shows the qualitative results. Coarse binning, such as 8 radial bins, covers a broad range of frequencies within each bin and mainly produces global changes, such as changes in overall brightness. By contrast, finer binning, such as 128 radial bins, produces more noticeable changes in image structure. These results suggest that binning resolution is one of the design choices that can affect the behavior of spectral correction. sections.heading: Appendix P Additional Qualitative Results
sections.text: Figures 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , and 21 show additional qualitative results on SDXL, PixArt- α \alpha , and SD3.5. Figures 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , and 27 show additional results under high guidance. Across these examples, our method produces more favorable outputs than the baselines. It mitigates artifacts observed in CFG, improves brightness and sharpness, and better preserves text-aligned visual content. Some outputs remain visually close to those of CFG. When intermediate spectra are already close to the analytic reference, our method applies only small spectral adjustments, helping preserve the quality already achieved by CFG. We recommend zooming in on the figures to examine fine-grained differences in visual quality and text alignment.

sections.heading: Analysis of Failure Cases.
sections.text: Despite the overall effectiveness of the proposed correction, the additional qualitative results also reveal two common failure patterns. These include cases where the correction only partially mitigates artifacts observed in CFG, and cases where improvements in visual quality or prompt alignment are accompanied by undesired changes in other aspects of the image. First, in the first example of Figure 17 , our method produces a cat with a more natural composition, but the generated cat still exhibits an abnormal tail structure. Similarly, in the fifth example of Figure 19 , the face of the person near the center is improved, while some details such as the hands remain unnatural. In these examples, our method retains much of the quality already achieved by CFG while refining some fine-grained details, though certain artifacts persist. In the last example of Figure 20 , our method improves visual quality over CFG, but some artifacts remain. Second, some cases show a trade-off between different aspects of generation quality. In the last example of Figure 23 , the overall color tone is improved, but the number of people increases, making the result less consistent with the text condition. In the last example of Figure 25 , the luggage shape becomes more natural, but the interaction between objects is weakened during the correction. These examples suggest that, while the proposed method can improve generation quality in many cases, there remains room for further improving its robustness.

sections.heading: Appendix Q Additional Discussion
sections.text: The proposed method improves guided generation by normalizing spectral deviations from the expected denoising dynamics. This correction keeps the guided trajectory closer to the spectral statistics induced by the forward process, which can improve image quality and prompt alignment. At the same time, the correction does not provide explicit feedback toward a desired semantic direction. As a result, its ability to control generation toward a specific target remains limited. More direct semantic control may require additional learning signals, such as external rewards or task-specific supervision, but the use of such signals introduces separate challenges. These observations suggest that more fundamental improvements may require aligning the denoising dynamics from the training stage. This direction calls for a deeper understanding of the representation space and generation dynamics formed by diffusion models. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is central to this success, but its lack of an explicit criterion makes it difficult to assess whether the guided trajectory is progressing as intended. To address this gap, we show that spectral alignment provides a principled criterion for understanding guidance behavior and improving guided diffusion sampling through adaptive correction. Our analysis identifies the spectra of intermediate states as an indicator of consistency with the expected spectral evolution of the forward process. Based on this observation, we introduce Spectral Correction Guidance , a method that corrects deviations from an analytic reference spectrum during sampling. The proposed method is training-free and applicable across diffusion backbones and conditional generation tasks without modifying the underlying model. Experiments demonstrate consistent gains in preference-based metrics over baseline guidance methods in text-to-image generation and improved generation quality over CFG on ImageNet. These improvements persist across a range of guidance scales and with fewer denoising steps. Our analyses and ablations provide insight into guidance behavior and how the proposed method affects generation quality. 1 Introduction Denoising diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) have shown strong generative capabilities across diverse domains ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) , including image synthesis ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ; Karras et al., 2022 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) . They exhibit stable convergence during training while modeling the reverse of a forward noising process that perturbs clean data toward a noise distribution. The learned reverse process captures rich data distributions, enabling sample generation through denoising from high to low noise levels. Building on this capability, diffusion models support open-ended conditional generation tasks such as text-to-image synthesis ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . Classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) has become a standard technique for steering sampling toward the target condition in diffusion models. As illustrated in Figures 1(a) and 1(b) , conditional sampling without guidance often fails to capture the target condition, whereas CFG improves both condition alignment and perceptual quality. These benefits depend on how guidance is applied along the denoising trajectory ( Hong et al., 2023 ; Karras et al., 2024 ; Sadat et al., 2024 ) . However, standard CFG uses a fixed guidance scale, limiting its ability to provide appropriate guidance at each denoising step ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) . Recent guidance methods aim to enhance the benefits of CFG while mitigating its adverse effects. They adjust the guidance strength across timesteps ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Malarz et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2025a ) , modify the direction of guidance with geometric constraints ( Sadat et al., 2025a ; Chung et al., 2024 ; Kwon et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2025b ) , or modulate guidance within predefined frequency bands ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Sadat et al., 2025b ; Song et al., 2026 ) . However, these benefits may not extend beyond the settings these methods are designed to address, such as high-guidance regimes. In Section 6.1 , experimental results show that these methods yield limited gains across a range of generation settings, where vanilla CFG remains a strong baseline. In this paper, we argue that these limitations arise from reliance on constraints or suppression rules without a criterion to guide correction along the denoising trajectory. However, defining such a criterion is challenging in the conventional spatial domain, since coordinate-based representations encode local structures and reflect sample-specific characteristics. To address this difficulty, we identify alignment between the power spectra of guided intermediate states and the expected spectra under the forward process as a key indicator of effective guidance. This provides a complementary perspective, capturing global patterns of diffusion dynamics along the denoising trajectory. Building on this observation, we propose Spectral Correction Guidance , a training-free method for correcting guided denoising trajectories according to the spectral dynamics of the diffusion process. We derive a criterion from the power-law spectral statistics of natural images ( Ruderman, 1997 ) , yielding a distributional reference that is not tied to individual samples or specific failure patterns. Based on this criterion, our method corrects deviations from the expected spectral behavior in intermediate states. The proposed correction enables adaptive adjustments across frequencies and timesteps without relying on a prescribed correction pattern. We further validate our method through extensive experiments on diverse conditional image generation tasks. In text-to-image generation, the proposed correction improves preference-based metrics across multiple backbones and guidance settings, indicating better text alignment and visual quality. In class-conditional generation, our method achieves lower FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and higher Inception Score ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) than CFG, even with fewer sampling steps. These results demonstrate that correcting spectral deviations during sampling can improve generation quality without additional training. Ablation studies examine how correction strength and the timestep range over which correction is applied affect generation outputs. We also discuss how the proposed method relates to existing guidance approaches from a spectral perspective. From a spectral perspective, we also examine how these strategies control distinct aspects of the guidance signal during denoising. Scheduled guidance scaling. Scheduled guidance scaling replaces the constant guidance scale w w with a predefined timestep-dependent schedule. Kynkäänniemi et al. (2024) restrict guidance to selected denoising intervals, while Malarz et al. (2025) and Jin et al. (2025a) adjust the guidance strength according to predefined functional forms. By Parseval’s theorem, adjusting the guidance scale at each timestep also modulates the Fourier-domain energy of the guidance term. In this sense, our method provides fine-grained scaling through spectral correction at each timestep and frequency. Geometry-aware guidance. Geometry-aware guidance methods constrain the magnitude ( Jin et al., 2025b ) or direction ( Sadat et al., 2025a ) of guided updates, or adjust sampling to reduce deviations from the data manifold ( Chung et al., 2024 ; Kwon et al., 2025 ) . Our method shares the goal of keeping guided trajectories consistent with the data distribution, but approaches it through spectral alignment with the forward marginals encountered during training. Frequency-based guidance. Frequency-based methods modulate guidance using predefined frequency partitions ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , applying different guidance strengths to separate bands ( Sadat et al., 2025b ) or suppressing selected frequencies ( Song et al., 2026 ) . Although these methods also consider spectral information, their adjustments follow band-specific rules. In contrast, our method adapts the correction at each frequency based on spectral deviations from an analytic reference. The relaxation analysis clarifies where spectral correction improves generation quality and where its continued application can degrade quality ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2025a ) . 7 Conclusion In this paper, we demonstrated that spectral alignment can serve as a practical criterion for understanding guidance behavior and improving guided diffusion sampling through principled correction. This perspective provides a basis for assessing whether guided trajectories remain consistent with the spectral dynamics induced by the forward process. We derived an analytic reference from natural image statistics and used it to correct spectral deviations along guided denoising trajectories. Building on this criterion, Spectral Correction Guidance is a training-free method applicable to diverse diffusion backbones and conditional generation tasks without modifying the underlying model. Experiments show that the proposed method improves generation quality across model architectures, guidance strengths, and reduced sampling budgets, while prior guidance strategies provide limited gains in common guidance settings.
